## 2.1.319
- Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0` to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
- Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1` turns on the server-side check even with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS` set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the `1` too
- Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
- Added the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND` environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
- Added `permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting` setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
- Added `/claude-api latency-optimize` to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
- Added the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS` environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
- Added spend for today, this week and this month to `/usage` for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
- Added `admin.pooled_conflict_rule` and `admin.pooled_priority_order` to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
- Added an optional `login_notice` setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
- Added `CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json` to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with `severity`, `time` and `message`, for log collectors that read the level from a field
- Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's `availableModels` also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
- Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no `desktopHome` that rely on `coworkTabEnabled: false` or `chatSessionRetentionDays`, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
- Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from `ant auth login`, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
- Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from `ant auth login`
- Added an "Earlier in this session" row to `/tasks` that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
- Added a note to `/loop` confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
- Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
- Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after `--resume`
- Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named `HEAD`
- Fixed `/diff` showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named `HEAD` at its top level
- Fixed the `/diff` pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
- Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running

article.title: Air in IDEs | JetBrains Air Documentation
article.text:
Air in IDEs
Air in IDEs is a plugin for agentic development. It gives you one place to start coding agents, follow what they are doing, and review the changes they make.
Air in IDEs is not an AI service of its own: it is a workspace for running coding agents. Agents come either from your existing local installations or from the agent registry. Depending on the agent and your setup, you can use JetBrains AI, a third-party provider account, or the agent's own authorization flow.
Watch a two-minute demo of Air in IDEs:
Why use Air in IDEs
Air in IDEs works with the agents, subscriptions, and IDE setup you already have:
Agents you already have installed
Air in IDEs detects the coding agents installed on your machine, such as Codex or Junie, the same way the IDE detects SDKs and build tools. A detected agent keeps the configuration it already uses.
Your existing subscriptions
Use the provider accounts and subscriptions you already have, or configure a provider in Air in IDEs. A JetBrains AI subscription is supported but not required.
IDE tools for agent changes
Agent sessions run in the same IDE as the rest of your work. Use code insight, refactorings, the debugger, and version control on the code an agent produces, and review, edit, or revert each change before you keep it.
Presets for different tasks
Save an agent, model, and operation mode as a named preset and reuse it instead of configuring each session. For example, keep one preset for small changes and another for larger, multi-step work.
Comparison with AI Assistant
JetBrains also ships AI Assistant – a collection of AI-powered features that includes coding agents, AI Chat, in-editor code completion, and code insights. Air in IDEs is a separate plugin and does not replace or disable AI Assistant.
Air in IDEs and AI Assistant cover different parts of AI-powered development:
Air in IDEs
AI Assistant
Primary focus
Provides an agentic workspace for running external or self-hosted coding agents and reusing their existing configurations, provider accounts, and subscriptions.
Provides JetBrains AI features, including AI Chat, in-editor code completion, next edit suggestions, code insights, and coding agents.
Agents
Detects coding agents already installed on your machine and makes them available in the IDE. You can also install ACP agents from the registry.
Includes a set of bundled agents and lets you install additional ACP-compatible agents when needed.
AI access
Depending on the agent and your setup, uses JetBrains AI, a provider configured in Air in IDEs, or an existing agent authorization. Air in IDEs does not provide AI models of its own and does not require a JetBrains AI subscription.
Connects to JetBrains AI models through a JetBrains AI subscription. Other supported activation options include your own API keys and provider accounts.
Workspace
Treats agents and their sessions as units of work. Sessions can use a structured chat or an agent's terminal interface and include presets, session diffs, parallel runs, and dedicated management views.
Integrates AI Chat, agents, and inline assistance into the editor and existing IDE tool windows as companion features.
How Air in IDEs works
Air in IDEs runs agents on your machine and communicates with ACP-compatible agents through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). CLI agents run in their own terminal interface. Because ACP is a standard interface, compatible agents can work without a dedicated integration.
Agents become available to Air in IDEs in two ways:
Local installations – agents already installed on your machine. Air in IDEs detects them and makes them available in the IDE.
The ACP agent registry – a catalog of ACP-compatible agents that you can browse and install with your consent. By default, Air in IDEs uses a JetBrains-provided registry.
A typical session looks like this:
You select an agent for the task.
You authorize the agent if it has no available authorization source yet.
You describe the task in natural language.

Nov 5
Feature

v1/images/generations

October, 2026
Oct 30
Update
v1/agents
v1/agents/sessions
You can now update the tools in an existing session in the Agents API public beta. Updates replace the full tool list. Function tools and MCP servers change on the next model call; built-in tools change by the next turn.
Context compaction now runs in the background by default. Set compaction.async to false for blocking compaction. Background compaction may increase token usage.

Oct 30
Feature
v1/agents/sessions
Added automatic review for eligible Agents API projects. Set the session's review field to "auto_review" to have a model approve or deny supported tool and permission requests based on conversation intent and risk. See the automatic review guide for supported requests, limitations, and additional token billing.
Oct 30
Feature
gpt-6-rosalind
Released GPT-6 Rosalind, bringing specialized biological reasoning with scientific tool use to complex life sciences research. Access is available to organizations approved for Rosalind Research through the trusted-access program for internal research by authorized users.
Oct 28
Feature
Eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business subscribers can now claim up to $500 per month in free API credits as a subscription benefit. Activate the benefit from ChatGPT or API Platform by linking an API organization you own. See API credits for ChatGPT subscribers for credit amounts, eligibility, and how to claim.
Oct 26
Feature
gpt-6.1-terra
v1/responses
v1/chat/completions
Released GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model for visual reasoning, precise computer use, and clear, natural writing.
See the GPT-6 guide for prompting and migration guidance.
Oct 23
Feature
v1/agents/automations
Added scheduled automations to the Agents API public beta. Schedule one-time or recurring tasks in new or existing sessions. Enable the automations tool to let an agent schedule its own follow-ups in the current session.
Oct 22
Update
gpt-6-luna
v1/decisions
The Decisions API is now generally available with gpt-6-luna. Cache shared input across requests for prompt-cache discounts, include images in individual question instructions, and pass structured data directly with input_json. Each request now supports up to 400 questions, increased from 200 in public beta. Review the changes since public beta.
Oct 21
Feature
You can now choose which service tiers projects can use in Platform settings. Organization settings can restrict service tiers for all projects. See service tier errors.
Oct 20
Feature
v1/responses
You can now choose 12-hour prompt caching in the API. 12-hour prompt caching keeps shared instructions, tools, and context cached longer to benefit from lower cached-input pricing, even when requests are hours apart. 12-hour cache writes cost 2.5x the input token price. Read more here.

# Agent Skills
**Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents.**
Skills encode the workflows, quality gates, and best practices that senior engineers use when building software. These ones are packaged so AI agents follow them consistently across every phase of development.
```
DEFINE PLAN BUILD VERIFY REVIEW SHIP
┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
│ Idea │ ───▶ │ Spec │ ───▶ │ Code │ ───▶ │ Test │ ───▶ │ QA │ ───▶ │ Go │
│Refine│ │ PRD │ │ Impl │ │Debug │ │ Gate │ │ Live │
└──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘
/spec /plan /build /test /review /ship
```
---
## Commands
9 slash commands that map to the development lifecycle. Each one activates the right skills automatically.
| What you're doing | Command | Key principle |
|-------------------|---------|---------------|
| Define what to build | `/spec` | Spec before code |
| Plan how to build it | `/plan` | Small, atomic tasks |
| Build incrementally | `/build` | One slice at a time |
| Prove it works | `/test` | Tests are proof |
| Set the quality bar | `/constraints` | Decide it once, enforce it everywhere |
| Review before merge | `/review` | Improve code health |
| Audit web performance | `/webperf` | Measure before you optimize |
| Simplify the code | `/code-simplify` | Clarity over cleverness |
| Ship to production | `/ship` | Faster is safer |
In Claude Code these install as plugin commands. Where a built-in command has the same name, as `/review` does, use the namespaced form: `/agent-skills:review`.
Want fewer manual steps once the spec exists? **`/build auto`** generates the plan and implements every task in a single approved pass — you approve the plan once, then it runs autonomously. It removes the human stepping *between* tasks, not the verification: every task is still test-driven and committed individually, and it pauses on failures or risky steps.
Skills also activate automatically based on what you're doing — designing an API triggers `api-and-interface-design`, building UI triggers `frontend-ui-engineering`, and so on.
---
## Quick Start
**Fastest path — any agent, one command.** The open [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) installs into 70+ agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Cline, and more):
```bash
npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills # install all 25 skills
npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --list # browse before installing
```
Or grab individual skills:
```bash
npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --skill code-review-and-quality # five-axis review before merge
npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --skill interview-me # requirements interrogation, one question at a time
npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --skill test-driven-development # red-green-refactor, enforced
```
> **Installing one skill?** A per-skill `npx` install copies only
> `skills//`, not the repo-level `references/` directory. The skill still
> works, but paths to supplementary shared checklists are unavailable. Use a
> whole-repo integration, clone the repository, or copy the needed checklist into
> a `references/` directory inside the installed skill. This portability gap is
> tracked in [#361](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/issues/361).
Prefer a native integration? Pick your tool below.
Claude Code (recommended)
**Marketplace install:**
```
/plugin marketplace add addyosmani/agent-skills
/plugin install agent-skills@addy-agent-skills
```
> **SSH errors?** The marketplace clones repos via SSH. If you don't have SSH keys set up on GitHub, either [add your SSH key](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-account) or use the full HTTPS URL to force HTTPS cloning during the marketplace-add step:
> ```bash
> /plugin marketplace add https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills.git
> /plugin install agent-skills@addy-agent-skills
> ```
>
> If `/plugin install` still fails with `git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey)` on…

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking…

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking…

Remote Agents
Section titled “Remote Agents”
Antigravity Remote Agents run your agent sessions and tools in an isolated,
Google-managed remote environment rather than on your local machine.
Because execution happens remotely, Remote Agents continue working on
long-running tasks and executing commands even when you close your browser, put
your laptop to sleep, or switch between desktop and mobile devices.
Remote Agents vs. Remote Control
Section titled “Remote Agents vs. Remote Control”
Antigravity provides two ways to work with agents remotely depending on where
your code and tools live. Use the following table to compare Remote Agents
and Remote Control:
FeatureRemote AgentsRemote Control
Execution environmentIsolated, Google-managed remote environmentYour own desktop workstation or server
Host machine requirementRuns independently; no local machine needs to stay onRequires your host machine to remain powered on and online
Workspace and filesRemote Resources (GitHub repositories, Google Drive files, and uploaded files)Local filesystem folders, local toolchains, and Git worktrees
Best forRepository tasks, mobile workflows, and background execution while awayTasks that require local hardware, local dev servers, or uncommitted local checkouts
Getting started
Section titled “Getting started”
You can launch and manage Remote Agents from the Antigravity App on your
desktop, from the Antigravity CLI in your terminal, or directly from any web
browser at antigravity.google.com.
Antigravity App
Antigravity CLI
Antigravity App
Section titled “Antigravity App”
Start in the Antigravity App
Section titled “Start in the Antigravity App”
To create a remote project alongside your local projects in the Antigravity App,
do the following:
In the left sidebar, click + next to Projects (or open the project
selector in the message box) and select New Remote Project.
(Optional) Click Add Resource to attach GitHub repositories, Google
Drive files, or uploaded files from your computer, and then click Next
(or Skip if you do not add any resources yet).
Enter a name in Set Project Name and click Create.
Select your remote project and send a prompt in the message box to start a
remote conversation.
You can also start a remote project directly from a GitHub repository in the
message box:
In the message box, click the project selector dropdown.
Select Remote > GitHub Repositories. If you have not connected your
GitHub account yet, click Connect GitHub to authorize access.
Choose a repository from the list. Antigravity automatically selects an
existing remote project for that repository or creates a new one.
Start on the web
Section titled “Start on the web”
To use Remote Agents from a desktop or mobile browser without installing a local
application, do the following:
Open your browser and navigate to
antigravity.google.com.
Sign in with a personal Google Account on an eligible plan (Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra).
Enter a prompt in the message box to start a standalone remote conversation,
or click Create Project next to Projects in the left sidebar to
configure a project with GitHub repositories, Google Drive files, or
uploaded files.
Switch between Remote Agents and Remote Control
Section titled “Switch between Remote Agents and Remote Control”
If you also use Remote Control to connect to local
Antigravity App or Antigravity CLI instances, use the instance switcher on
antigravity.google.com (in the left sidebar
above Settings on desktop browsers, or in the top bar on mobile) to switch
between Remote Conversations and any of your connected host machines.
